description: Charles 'Babe' Adams (1882-1968) played all but a few months of his 19 years in the majors with the Pittsburgh Pirates. Known as an outstanding control pitcher, the right hander had a career average of 1.29 walks per nine innings pitched, ranking as the second lowest in the 20th century. When his career ended in 1926, Adams had posted 194 wins and 140 losses, winning 20 games twice. He threw three complete game victories against Detroit en route to a 1909 Pirates' World Series championship.

title: Baker, Frank 1918
description: Pictured here as a New York Yankee, third baseman Frank Baker (1886-1963) was the top slugger in baseball’s deadball era. He earned the moniker Home Run Baker because of two clutch home runs that helped win games two and three of the 1911 World Series, which ended in a championship for his Philadelphia Athletics. Baker was the American League home run king four consecutive years, hitting 11 round-trippers in 1911, 10 in 1912, 12 in 1913, and 9 in 1914. His 13-year playing career (1908-1922) included three World Series championships, all with the A's. He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1955.

title: Larry Doby, 1951
description: Pictured here at Cleveland Municipal Stadium, Larry Doby (1923-2003) was the first African-American player in the American League, making his debut with the Cleveland Indians in July 1947. Doby and teammate Satchel Paige were the first African-American players to win a World Series championship, helping the Indians prevail in 1948. Also in that year, his first as the team's full-time centerfielder, Doby batted .301. During his career (1947-1959), he made the all-star team seven consecutive years, and hit 20 or more home runs in eight straight years, including 32 each in 1952 and 1954, when he led the American League. Larry Doby was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1998.

title: Doyle, Larry 1919
author: Central News Photo Service
description: Pictured here as a member of the New York Giants, Larry Doyle (1886-1974) played most of his 14-year career with the Giants, helping the team win three straight pennants in 1911-13. As the son of a coal miner, Doyle himself worked five years in the mines and played semi-pro baseball prior to reaching the majors in 1907. In 1911, having established himself as an aggressive player and team leader, he was known to have said, “It’s great to be young and a New York Giant.” The second baseman won a batting title in 1915, hitting .320. When he retired in 1920, Doyle had achieved a .408 slugging percentage, tops by a National League second baseman at the time. His career batting average was .290.

title: Cleveland Indians 1954 American League Champions
description: This autographed team photo of the 1954 American League champion Cleveland Indians includes players, coaches and some associated personnel. The Indians were a regular season juggernaut in 1954, winning 111 games and losing just 43. The World Series was a different story, as the team went down to defeat four games to none to the New York Giants. The 1954 World Series was the last one played at Cleveland Municipal Stadium.

title: Cuccinello, Anthony 1957
description: Pictured here in his Cleveland Indians uniform in March 1957, Tony Cuccinello (1907–1995) coached with the Indians during the 1952-1956 seasons. As a player, he was a three-time all-star during his major league career (1930-1945). He played for the Cincinnati Reds, Brooklyn Dodgers, Boston Bees, Boston Braves and Chicago White Sox. He led National League second basemen in assists and double plays three times. Cuccinello batted .300 or better five times, posting a career best .315 in 1931. He hit .308 for the Chicago White Sox in 1945, but lost the American League batting title to Snuffy Stirnweiss by .000087 of a percentage point, making it the closest batting race in major league history. After his playing days, he managed and coached in the minors, and then returned to the majors, coaching for the Cincinnati Reds, the Indians, the Chicago White Sox and the 1968 World Series champions, the Detroit Tigers.

title: Luke Easter, 1952
description: Pictured here as a member of the Cleveland Indians, Luke Easter (ca. 1915-1979) made a brief debut in Major League Baseball in 1949 with the Indians, following success in the semi-pros, Negro leagues, and Triple-A. As a 34-year-old rookie in 1950, he became the Indians starting first baseman, and hit 20 home runs, drove in 107 runs, and batted .280. In the same year, he hit a Municipal Stadium record 477-ft. blast to the upper deck in right field. Mickey Mantle was the only other player to match that, doing so in 1960. Easter had 27 homers in 1951, and 31 in 1952. Injuries and age slowed the 6’4”, 240-lb. slugger, and he retired from the major leagues after the 1954 season. He continued to play professionally in Triple-A, retiring as a player in 1963. Easter was shot and killed in Cleveland in 1979, while transporting money from payroll checks for his co-workers at TRW. In memoriam, Woodland Hills Park was renamed Luke Easter Park in 1980.

title: Hoskins, David 1953
author: Bottomer, Fred
description: Shown here in a Cleveland Indians uniform, pitcher David Hoskins (1925-1970) played two years with the Indians. He appeared in 26 games in the 1953 season, winning nine and losing three, and batting .259. In 1954, he pitched in only 14 games, and had a win-loss record of 0-1 on a team that featured a number of dominant pitchers. Earlier in his baseball career, Hoskins had been a star in the Negro Leagues. Playing for the Homestead Grays in 1944, he was switched from pitcher to outfield and batted .324 on a team with such hitting stars as Buck Leonard and Josh Gibson. In 1945, he starred as both a pitcher and hitter for the Grays. In 1950-1952, Hoskins played in the minor leagues. As a member of the Dallas Eagles in 1952, he was the first African-American to play in the Texas League. In that year, he won 22 games as a pitcher, and batted .328. After some other stops, he returned to the Eagles in 1958, and had 17 victories as a pitcher. David Hoskins was inducted into the Texas League Hall of Fame in 2004.

title: Lemon, Bob 1948
description: Pictured here as a member of the Cleveland Indians, Bob Lemon (1920-2000) was a player and manager in the major leagues. He began his career as a position player with the Cleveland Indians, playing briefly in the years 1941 and 1942. He then served three years in the United States Navy during World War II. After 1946, his first full year in the majors, Lemon was converted to pitcher. In his 13-year career, the right-hander posted 207 wins and 108 losses, and had a no-hitter against the Detroit Tigers in 1948. His 37 home runs as a pitcher rank him second in home runs for pitchers in the major leagues, one behind the 38 hit by Wes Ferrell. Lemon won 20 games seven times, and was also a seven-time member of the all-star team. He won a World Series as a player with the Indians in 1948, and was the manager of the triumphant Chicago White Sox in the 1978 World Series. He also managed the New York Yankees and the Kansas City Royals. Lemon was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1976.

title: Mathewson, Christy 1916
author: Underwood & Underwood
description: Pictured here on his first day as the manager of the Cincinnati Reds, Christy Mathewson (1880-1925) was one of the all-time great pitchers in the major leagues. Before making his debut with the New York Giants in July 1900, Mathewson played minor league baseball in 1899-1900, winning 20 games and losing only two in the latter year. He’d left college in 1899 after two years at Bucknell University, where “Matty” played three sports, was elected class president, and participated in the glee club and a literary society. Over his professional baseball career, Mathewson won 30 or more games four times, and 20 or more games thirteen times, reaching 373 wins over 17 years. In a 37-win season in 1908 with the New York Giants, he posted an E.R.A. of 1.43. In the 1905 World Series, he pitched three shutouts in six days against the Philadelphia Athletics, helping the Giants win the championship. Mathewson was traded from the Giants to the Cincinnati Reds in 1916, his last year as a player, and went on to manage the Reds during that season and through 1918. He enlisted in the U.S. Army in 1918 for World War I and, while training in France, fell victim to a poisonous gas accident. He later developed tuberculosis, leading to his death in 1925 at the age of 47. Mathewson was one of the “five immortals” in the 1936 inaugural class of the Baseball Hall of Fame. The others were Babe Ruth, Ty Cobb, Walter Johnson and Honus Wagner.

title: Mitchell, Dale 1952
description: Shown here as a member of the Cleveland Indians, Dale Mitchell (1921-1987) was an outfielder in Major League Baseball in 1946-1956. He played all but 19 of his 1,127 regular season games with the Indians. He was with the Brooklyn Dodgers toward the end of the 1956 season. Known as an outstanding contact hitter, the leftfielder had a career batting average of .312. In 1948, he hit a career high .336 with 204 hits, helping the Indians win the World Series. Mitchell made the all-star team twice.

title: Pope, David 1954
description: Shown here as a member of the Cleveland Indians, David Pope (1921-1999) played four years in Major League Baseball, beginning in 1952 with the Indians. He was traded to the Baltimore Orioles in 1955, and then traded back to the Indians in 1956, where he ended his Major League career. After that, he returned to the minors, playing until 1961. The centerfielder’s best big league year was in 1955, when he had 86 hits, 38 runs, 13 doubles, 4 triples, 7 home runs, and 52 RBI. Pope also played one year in the Negro leagues, and participated in the 1954 World Series. He spent a number of his post-baseball years working for the Cleveland Recreation Department at the Cory Recreation Center. David Pope is buried in Lake View Cemetery in Cleveland.

He spent a number of his post-baseball years working for the Cleveland Recreation Department at the Cory Recreation Center. David Pope is buried in Lake View Cemetery in Cleveland.

title: Tomanek, Dick 1957
description: Pictured here in his Cleveland Indians uniform, southpaw pitcher Dick Tomanek (1931- ) played Major League Baseball with the Indians in 1953-1954, and in 1957-1958. He was a member of the Kansas City Athletics in 1958-1959. The Avon Lake, Ohio native had a career win-loss record of 10-10.

title: Cleveland Indians 1923
description: The 1923 Cleveland Indians were led by player-manager Tris Speaker, who batted .380 and tied Babe Ruth for the American League RBI title with 130. Shortstop Joe Sewell hit .353 and knocked in 109 runs. George Uhle was the team’s leading starter, posting 26 wins and 16 losses, while Stan Coveleski won the ERA title with 2.76. The Indians finished the year at 82-71, just behind the Tigers, but far behind the pennant-winning New York Yankees.

title: Dente, Samuel 1957
description: Pictured in a Cleveland Indians uniform, shortstop Samuel Dente (1922–2002) played with five teams in his Major League Baseball career (1947-1955), including the Indians in 1954-1955. He signed with the Boston Red Sox as an amateur free agent prior to the 1941 season, and played in the minors until 1944, when he went to serve in World War II. Dente was a .252 hitter lifetime, with 214 RBI in 745 major league games. He played with the Indians in the 1954 World Series.

title: Dyck, Jim 1954
author: Bottomer, Fred
description: Pictured here in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Jim Dyck (1922–1999) played with four teams in the  major leagues in 1951-1956, including a very brief stint with the Indians in 1954. In 330 games over his career, he had a .246 batting average, with 26 homers and 114 runs batted in. He was primarily a third baseman and leftfielder, but played every position, except pitcher and catcher. Jim Dyck served as a naval pilot in World War II.

title: Garcia, Mike 1952
description: Mike Garcia (1923-1986) had a 14-year pitching career in the majors, most notably with the Indians in 1948-1959. In the early 1950s, he was one of the “Big Four” on the Indians staff, with the others being Bob Lemon, Early Wynn, and Bob Feller. Nicknamed the Big Bear, the right-handed power pitcher had a career win-loss record of 142-97. He posted two 20-win seasons, and was a three-time All-Star. Mike Garcia served in U.S. Army for three years during World War II.

title: Ginsberg, Joe [Myron] 1953
description: Pictured here in his catcher's crouch in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Myron Nathan (Joe) Ginsberg (1926–2012) played 13 years in the majors with seven teams, including the Indians (1953-1954). His career began in 1948 and ended in 1962, when he had a brief stint as an original member of the New York Mets. Ginsberg had a lifetime batting average of .241 in 1,716 at bats over 695 games. He was a member of the American League champion Indians in 1954.

title: Ginsberg, Joe [Myron] 1954
description: Pictured here in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Myron Nathan (Joe) Ginsberg (1926–2012) played 13 years in the majors with seven teams, including the Indians (1953-1954). His career began in 1948 and ended in 1962, when he had a brief stint as an original member of the New York Mets. Ginsberg had a lifetime batting average of .241 in 1,716 at bats over 695 games. He was a member of the American League champion Indians in 1954.

title: Harder, Mel 1957
description: Mel Harder (1909-2002) was a pitcher with the Cleveland Indians for twenty years, beginning in 1928. After his retirement as a player, he was the team’s pitching coach for another sixteen years, and then went on to coach with four other teams before finally retiring. The four-time All-Star right-hander won 223 games in his career, and led the American League in earned run average six times. He won 20 games twice and 15 games eight times. His 582 games pitched still stands as a team record. He was the pitching coach on the 1948 World Series champion Indians. Mel Harder died in Chardon, Ohio at age 93.

title: Hegan, Jim 1955
description: Shown here in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Jim Hegan (1920-1984) was an outstanding defensive major league catcher in his 17-year career (1941-1942 and 1946-1960). He played with five teams, most notably spending 13 years as a member of the Indians. He served in the United States Coast Guard in World War II. Although not an elite hitter, he was so skilled and intelligent behind the plate that he ended up a five-time All-Star anyway. He was a key player in the Indians’ 1948 World Series championship, handling a dominant pitching staff that included Bob Feller, Bob Lemon and Gene Bearden. Jim Hegan had a career fielding percentage of .990.

title: Devore, Joshua 1913
author: Schmidt, J.R.
description: Pictured here in a New York Giants uniform, Joshua (Josh) Devore (1887-1954) played with four teams in his seven years in the major leagues (1908-1914). Known as the Seelyville Speed Demon, the 5-foot, 6-inch outfielder was a top bunter and base stealer, totaling 160 base thefts in his career, including 61 in 1911. He hit .277 in the majors. Devore played with the Giants' 1911 and 1912 pennant-winning teams, and the 1914 World Series champion Boston Braves.

title: Lopez, Al with Tris Speaker
description: Shown here in a Cleveland Indians uniform with fellow Hall-of-Famer Tris Speaker, Al Lopez (1908-2005) was a successful catcher and manager in the major leagues. As a player in 1928-1947, he played with four teams, including the Indians in 1947. For his career, Lopez hit .261, with 1,547 hits and 652 RBI. He was a two-time all-star. When he retired as a player after the 1947 season, he’d played in 1,918 games as a catcher, a major league record at the time. As a manager, he had a .584 winning percentage, with a record of 1,410 wins and 1,004 losses. In 1949-1964, when the New York Yankees won all but two American League pennants, only the Al Lopez-managed teams in 1954 (Indians) and 1959 (Chicago White Sox) stopped the streak. He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1977.

title: Majeski, Hank 1955
description: Shown here in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Hank Majeski (1916–1991) played with six major league teams in a career that spanned 1939-1941 and 1946-1955. He was a member of the U.S. Coast Guard in 1943 during World War II, and missed the 1943-1945 seasons. Majeski was a .279 career hitter and played on the 1954 pennant-winning Indians. The slick-fielding third-baseman had a record-setting year in 1947, achieving a fielding percentage of .988. In 1948, he batted .310, hit 12 homers, and knocked in 120 runs. He had the league’s best fielding percentage again, this time with .975. Also in 1948, he hit six doubles in a doubleheader.

title: Narleski, Ray 1958
description: Shown in his Cleveland Indians uniform, Ray Narleski (1928–2012) was a star reliever in Major League Baseball, playing with the Indians in 1954-1958, and the Detroit Tigers in 1959. Narleski had a win-loss record of 43-33 in the majors, posting 58 career saves in 702 innings, with an earned run average of 3.60. Armed with a top-flight fastball and good breaking pitches, he was an American League All-Star in 1956 and 1958. Narleski was on the Indians' 1954 World Series squad.

title: Regalado, Rudy  1954
author: Bottomer, Fred
description: Standing on third base with glove ready, Cleveland Indians infielder Rudolph Valentino (Rudy) Regalado (1930- ) played with the Indians in his three-year major league career (1954-1956). He had a career batting average of .249 in 288 plate appearances, and participated in the 1954 World Series.

title: Rosen, Al  1952
description: Al Rosen (1924- ) played 10 years in the majors, all with the Indians (1947-1956). The third baseman made the All-Star team four times, and led the American League in home runs and RBIs two times each. He was league MVP in 1953, hitting 43 home runs and driving in 145 runs. For his career, Rosen hit .285, with 192 homers and 717 runs batted in. He was a member of the Indians in their World Series championship year in 1948, and was a major contributor to the team’s American League championship in 1954. After retiring as a player, he later returned to Major League Baseball as an executive for several teams. He was club president and CEO of the New York Yankees in 1978-1979. The Yankees won the 1978 World Series. He was general manager of the San Francisco Giants in 1985-1992. The Giants won the National League pennant in 1989. Al Rosen served with the U.S. Navy in World War II.

title: Santiago, Jose 1954
description: Pitcher José Santiago (1928- ) made his major league debut with the Indians in 1954, and also played with the team in 1955. He played with the Kansas City Athletics in 1956. The right-hander had a career win-loss record of 3-2 in the majors in 27 appearances. He played in the Negro leagues in 1947-1948 as a member of the New York Cubans. In 11 years in the minor leagues, Santiago won 112 games.

title: Smith, Al  1955
author: Bottomer, Fred
description: Pictured here in a Cleveland Indians uniform crossing home plate, Al Smith (1928–2002) played 12 productive seasons in the American League (1953-1964) with four teams, including the Indians (1953–1957, 1964). The outfielder/third baseman had career totals of 164 home runs, 676 runs batted in, and a batting average of .272. He was a two-time All-Star, and played on two American League pennant winners, the Indians in 1954, and Chicago White Sox in 1959. He also played in the Negro Leagues, having been signed at age 17 by the Cleveland Buckeyes.

title: Wertz, Victor
description: Pictured here in his Cleveland Indians uniform stretching for a throw at first base, Vic Wertz (1925–1983) was a four-time All-Star in his 17-year major league career (1947-1963). He played with six teams, including the Indians in 1954-1958. In his career, the first baseman/outfielder batted .277, hit 266 home runs, and had 1,178 runs batted in. He finished in the top 15 in Most Valuable Player voting five times, and was in the top 10 in the American League in homers seven times. In the Indians' losing effort in the 1954 World Series against the New York Giants, Wertz hit the blast to deep centerfield that Willie Mays caught with his back to home plate, in what is now one of the most iconic plays in major league history. Vic Wertz was also a World War II veteran.

title: Westlake, Wally
description: Pictured in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Wally Westlake (!920- ) played with six teams in his 10 years in the majors, including the Indians in 1952-1955. The journeyman infielder/outfielder slugged 127 home runs in his career, including 97 with his first team, the Pittsburgh Pirates (1947-1951). He batted in 539 runs and hit .272 in 958 total games. Westlake made the National League All-Star team in 1951 as a member of the St. Louis Cardinals. He participated in the 1954 World Series with the Indians.

title: Coombs, John
description: John (“Jack”) Coombs (1882-1957) pitched with three teams in a very productive major league career. As a member of the Philadelphia Athletics (1906-1914), the Colby College graduate played on World Series championship teams in 1910 and 1911, and was a three-time winner in the 1910 series. Also in 1910, he won 31 games during the regular season, and lost only nine, posting 13 shutouts, He also had a consecutive scoreless innings streak of 53 innings in that year. He had 28 wins in 1911. Coombs' career win-loss record was 158-110, with a 2.78 ERA. He also played with the Brooklyn Dodgers (1915-1918) and Detroit Tigers (1920). Among his other achievements, Jack Coombs coached the Duke University baseball team to 382 wins over 22 years (1929-1952).

title: Davis, George
description: Pictured here in a New York Giants uniform, George Davis (1870–1940) had a prolific 20-year Major League Baseball career. He played with the Giants in 1893-1901 and 1903, and was a player-manager with them in 1895 and 1900-1901. He also played with the Cleveland Spiders (1890-1892) and Chicago White Sox (1902 and 1904-1909). Skilled as a shortstop, third baseman and outfielder, Davis batted over .300 in nine consecutive seasons, scored 100 or more runs in five seasons, and had over 100 RBI in three campaigns. He was the National League batting champ in 1897, hitting .353. In 1906, as a member of the White Sox, he won a World Series title. Davis had a career batting average of .295. He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1998.

title: Dinneen, William 1914
description: Pictured here in his umpire's attire, William Dinneen (or Dineen) (1876-1955) had a 12-year major league pitching career with four teams, posting a win-loss record of 170-177. As a member of the Boston Americans in the inaugural 1903 World Series, Dinneen won three games against the Pittsburgh Pirates, including the first two shutouts in series history. He won 65 games in his first three years in the majors, averaging over 300 innings pitched per year and a 2.49 ERA. In 1904, Dinneen threw an American League record 37 straight complete games, and set a second related record of 335 2/3 innings pitched without being relieved. In winning 23 games that year, he finished every game he started. After his playing career, Bill Dinneen was an American League umpire in 1909-1937.

title: Faber, Urban 1927
description: Urban (Red) Faber (1888-1976) played exclusively with the Chicago White Sox in his 20-year major league career. At the time of his retirement in 1933, he was the American League’s last legal spitball pitcher. During his career, Faber won 254 games and posted an ERA of 3.15. Mainly a starter for the White Sox, he led the league in complete games in 1921 and 1922, with 32 and 31, respectively. He had three victories in the 1917 World Series, helping the Sox win the championship. He was also with the team during the 1919 Black Sox World Series scandal, but didn’t play because of injuries. Red Faber was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1964.

title: Schaefer, Herman (Germany) 1915
description: Herman (Germany) Schaefer (1876-1919) was known as one of Major League Baseball's great pranksters. The second baseman played 15 seasons with six teams (1901-1918), and had a career batting average of .257. His name is associated with a rule change that occurred because he stole first base. Possibly in 1908, according to some, Schaefer was standing on first, and another runner was on third. Schaefer ran to steal second base, hoping the catcher would throw to second, and that the runner on third would break for home plate. When the catcher didn’t throw, Schaefer ran back to first, and still didn’t get a throw. A second attempt at the delayed double steal worked, with the runner from third crossing home safely as the catcher threw to second. In 1920, a rule was added to prevent a player from running the bases in reverse order once he had legally occupied another base. Among other antics, Schaefer was known to have worn a raincoat to his position in the infield when it was raining, and to have carried a lantern onto the field when he thought it was getting too dark to play.

title: Snodgrass, Fred
description: Pictured in a New York Giants uniform, Fred Snodgrass (1887–1974) had a nine-year career in the majors as an outfielder, playing with the Giants (1908-1915) and Boston Braves (1915-1916). Known as a good fielder and base-stealer, he was a .275 career hitter, and achieved a .321 average in 1910. Snodgrass played in three straight World Series in 1911-1913, with the Giants losing all three. In the 1912 series, he was known for the “$30,000 Muff” because he dropped a fly ball in the 10th inning of the last game, leading to a Boston Red Sox comeback and, ultimately, the championship. The $30,000 was the difference between the winner and loser shares. The costly error diminished a spectacular, run-saving catch Snodgrass had made immediately after the drop.

title: Wood, Joe 1913
description: Shown here in a Boston Red Sox uniform, Joe Wood (1889-1985) played with the Red Sox (1908-1915) and Cleveland Indians (1917-1922) in his major league career. He was primarily a pitcher with the Red Sox. In 1912, Smoky Joe posted a sensational win-loss record of 34-5, struck out 258 batters, and had an ERA of 1.91. His career marks were 116 wins and 57 losses. An injury eventually ended his ability to be an effective pitcher. He was mainly an outfielder with the Indians. As a hitter, Wood’s career average was .283. He played on World Series winners in 1912, 1915, and 1920. After his retirement, he went on to be the head coach of the Yale University baseball team, winning 283 games over 20 years.

title: Evers, Johnny P. 1921
description: Pictured here as the manager of the Chicago Cubs, Johnny Evers (1881–1947) was a second baseman with the Cubs, Boston Braves, and Philadelphia Phillies in a playing career spanning 1902-1917. He managed the Cubs in 1913 and 1921, and the White Sox in 1924. The fiery 125-lb. Evers batted .270 in his career, and had an on-base percentage of .356. He was part of the Cubs’ famous double-play combination, “Tinker-to-Evers-to-Chance,” which was immortalized in the poem Baseball's Sad Lexicon by Franklin Adams. Evers played on World Series championship teams with the Cubs in 1907 and 1908, and the Braves in 1914, when the Miracle Braves swept the Phildelphia Athletics. Also in 1914, he was the National League’s MVP. Johnny Evers was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1946.

title: Evers, Johnny P. 1921
description: Johnny Evers, the manager of the Chicago Cubs, shakes hands with team majority owner and chewing gum magnate William Wrigley, Jr. Evers (1881–1947) was a second baseman with the Cubs, Boston Braves, and Philadelphia Phillies in a playing career spanning 1902-1917. He managed the Cubs in 1913 and 1921, and the White Sox in 1924. The fiery 125-lb. Evers batted .270 in his career, and had an on-base percentage of .356. He was part of the Cubs’ famous double-play combination, “Tinker-to-Evers-to-Chance,” which was immortalized in the poem Baseball's Sad Lexicon by Franklin Adams. Evers played on World Series championship teams with the Cubs in 1907 and 1908, and the Braves in 1914, when the “Miracle Braves” swept the Philadelphia Athletics. Also in 1914, Evers was the National League MVP. Johnny Evers was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1946.

title: Avila, Roberto 1957
description: Bobby Avila (1924-2004) played second base with four major league teams, most notably the Cleveland Indians in 1949-1958. The three-time all-star won the American League batting title in 1954 with a .341 average. For his career, Avila hit .281, with 80 homers and 467 RBI. He was a member of the Indians’ 1954 World Series squad.

title: Chakales, Bob 1953
description: Cleveland Indians pitcher Bob Chakales (1927-2010) is pictured here in his windup. Chakales played with five clubs in the major leagues, beginning with the Indians in 1951-1954. The right-hander pitched as both a starter and reliever, posting a career win-loss record of 15-25, with an ERA of 4.54. In 1954, he had five wins and 47 strikeouts, both career highs.

title: Glynn, Bill 1954
description: Pictured here in his Cleveland Indians uniform, Bill Glynn (1925-2013) played first base with the Philadelphia Phillies (1949) and the Indians (1952-1954). He batted .249 in his career, with 170 hits, 10 home runs, and 56 RBI.

title: Gowdy, Hank 1921
description: Pictured here as a member of the Boston Braves, Hank Gowdy (1889–1966) was a catcher and first baseman in the major leagues with the New York Giants and Braves. He played with each team two different times in 1910-1930. He was a member of the 1914 World Series champion Braves, batting a clutch .545 in the series, and hitting the only home run. Known as a strong defensive catcher, Gowdy hit .270 in his career, and had 322 runs batted in. He became the first big league player to enlist in World War I and, as a member of the 166th Infantry Regiment of the Ohio National Guard, was involved in the brutal trench warfare in France. After his playing career, Gowdy coached with three different teams in the majors. He enlisted in World War II, and was commissioned a major in the United States Army. He received votes in 17 years for induction into the Baseball Hall of Fame, but was never inducted.

title: Hooper, Bob 1955
description: Pictured here in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Bob Hooper (1922-1980) pitched with the Philadelphia Athletics, the Indians, and the Cincinnati Redlegs in his major league career (1950-1955). The Learnington, Ontario native won 15 games with the last-place Athletics in his rookie year. Later in his career, the right-hander became a relief pitcher. His career win-loss record was 40-41, with an ERA of 4.80. After his playing days, Hooper managed Baltimore Orioles’ farm teams, and did some scouting for the New York Mets.

title: Houtteman, Art 1957
description: Pictured here in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Art Houtteman (1927-2003) played 12 seasons in Major League Baseball with the Indians, Detroit Tigers and Baltimore Orioles. His career win-loss record was 87-91. He had 14 shutouts and 78 complete games. The right-hander went to spring training with the Tigers in 1945 at the age of 17. Houtteman was a member of the American League all-star team in 1950, when he won 19 regular season games for the Tigers.

title: Kennedy, Bob 1950
author: Somers, Arthur A.
description: Pictured in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Bob Kennedy (1920-2005) played with five teams in a major league career that spanned 1939-1957, minus three years in which he served in the military in World War II. As a member of the Indians in 1948-1954, the third baseman/outfielder was part of the team’s last World Series championship in 1948. He played 10 years in different stints with the Chicago White Sox. A career .254 batter, Kennedy hit 63 home runs and drove in 514 runs. In 1950, his best offensive season, he batted .291 and had 157 hits. Following his playing days, Bob Kennedy managed the Chicago Cubs and Oakland Athletics.

title: McGraw, John 1916
author: Underwood & Underwood
description: Shown left to right: manager of the New York Giants, John McGraw; Giants infielder and ex-player/manager of the Cincinnati Reds, Buck Herzog; and current manager of the Reds, Christy Mathewson. The photo was taken at the Polo Grounds, and marked Mathewson's first appearance there as the Reds' manager. John McGraw (1873-1934) was an outstanding dead-ball era player, and one of Major League Baseball's great managers. He played with the Baltimore Orioles, St. Louis Cardinals and the Giants in 1891-1906, although actually playing very little after 1902. McGraw had a lifetime batting average of .334, with 436 stolen bases, and a .466 on-base percentage. The fiery infielder combined bat control, speed and intelligence to become a feared leadoff hitter, batting over .320 nine straight times, and leading the National League in runs and walks twice. As a manager, he led the Giants to World Series championships in 1905, 1921 and 1922, and was on 10 pennant winners. His career managerial record was 2,763 wins and 1,948 losses, ranking him second in wins behind Connie Mack. John McGraw was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1937.

title: McGraw, John 1918
description: Pictured here as manager of the New York Giants, John McGraw (1873-1934) was an outstanding dead-ball era player, and one of Major League Baseball's great managers. title: Mossi, Don 1958
description: Pictured here in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Don Mossi (1929- ) pitched with four American League teams in his career (1954-1965), including the Indians in 1954-1958. The lefty control pitcher had a career earned run average of 3.43, with 101 wins, and 50 saves. As a member of the Detroit Tigers in 1961, he posted a win-loss record of 15-7, and had a 2.96 ERA. Mossi made the American League all-star team in 1957. His career fielding percentage was an outstanding .990.

title: Naragon, Hal 1954
author: Knipper, Clayton
description: Hal Naragon (1928- ) had a 10-year major league career as a catcher. The Zanesville, Ohio native played with the Cleveland Indians in 1951 and 1954-1959, and was a member of the 1954 team, which lost the World Series to the New York Giants. In 1952-1953, he served in the Marines. Naragon also played with the Washington Senators/Minnesota Twins (1959-1962). He hit .266 in his career, with 262 hits and 87 runs batted in. After his playing days, Hal Naragon was a bullpen coach with the Twins, as well as with the 1968 World Series champion Detroit Tigers.

title: Plank, Edward 1913
author: Underwood & Underwood
description: Edward (Eddie) Plank (1875-1926) is pictured here in his Philadelphia Athletics uniform warming up before the second game of the 1913 World Series. Plank pitched with three teams in a 17-year major league career. As a member of the Athletics (1901-1914), he was part of three World Series championships, and was the winning pitcher in the deciding game of the 1913 series against the New York Giants. The deadball era ace had a career win-loss record of 326-194, with an earned run average of 2.35 and 2,246 strikeouts. He posted 20 or more wins in eight seasons, and threw 66 shutouts. In 1915, he won 21 games pitching with the Federal League’s St. Louis Terriers. In his last start in 1917, while with the St. Louis Browns, the southpaw pitched against Walter Johnson, losing 1-0 in 11 innings. Eddie Plank was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1946.

title: Strickland, George 1954
author: Bottomer, Fred
description: Pictured in a Cleveland Indians uniform at the batting cage, George Strickland (1926-2010) played with the Pittsburgh Pirates (1950-1952) and Indians (1952-1957, 1959-1960) in his 10-year big league career. A lifetime .224 hitter, Strickland batted a career best .284 in his first full season with the Indians in 1953. His .976 fielding percentage in 1955 led all major league shortstops. After his playing days, George Strickland worked as a scout, third base coach and interim manager for the Indians. He also coached with the Minnesota Twins and Kansas City Royals.

title: Wynn, Early 1954
author: Knipper, Clayton
description: Shown here at Muncipal Stadium in his Cleveland Indians uniform, Early Wynn (1920-1999) was one of the American League’s top pitchers in his 23-year career. He played with the Washington Senators, the Indians (1949-1957), and the Chicago White Sox. The eight-time all-star right-hander had a career win-loss record of 300-244, with 2,334 strikeouts and an ERA of 3.54. Known as an intimidating presence on the mound, Wynn was the Cy Young winner in 1959, posting 22 wins that year with an earned run average of 3.17. He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1972.

title: Newhouser, Hall 1954
description: Pictured in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Hal Newhouser (1921-1998) was an American League pitcher with the Detroit Tigers (1939-1953), and the Indians (1954-1955). His career win-loss record was 207-150; his earned run average was 3.06. He won the American League MVP awards in 1944 and 1945. In the latter year, he led the league in wins with 25, strikeouts (212) and earned run average (1.81). Also in 1945, his Tigers were World Series champions. He was the winning pitcher in two of those games. The seven-time all-star was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1992.

title: BB-Cicotte, Edward
description: Edward Cicotte (1884–1969) pitched for the Chicago White Sox, Detroit Tigers, and Boston Red Sox in his 14 years in the major leagues. Nicknamed "Knuckles," the knuckleballer won 209 games and lost 148 in his career, posting a 2.38 earned run average. He had 28 wins in 1917, and 29 in 1919. Due to his alleged participation in the Black Sox scandal in the 1919 World Series, Cicotte was one of eight players to receive a lifetime ban from professional baseball.

title: P-Kerr, Dickey
description: Dickey Kerr (1893-1963) pitched for the Chicago White Sox in 1919-1921. He had 13 wins as a rookie. He won 21 and 19 games, respectively, in the next two years. He won both his starts in the 1919 World Series. Eight of his teammates received permanent suspensions for conspiring to fix the series, but Dickey was known as one of the White Sox who played honestly. After a contract disagreement, he quit major league baseball in 1922, and was put on the permanent ineligible list. He was reinstated in 1925 and attempted a comeback with the White Sox, pitching mainly out of the bullpen. His career won-loss record was 53-34.

title: BB-Cobb, Ty
author: Underwood & Underwood
description: Shown here in his United State Army uniform, Tyrus "Ty" Cobb (1886–1961) was a major league outfielder who played 22 seasons with the Detroit Tigers (1905-1926), including the last six as a player-manager. He finished his career with the Philadelphia Athletics in 1927-1928. The Georgia native, known as the “Georgia Peach,” had a career batting average of .366, with 4,189 hits, and 897 stolen bases, according to baseball-reference.com. Cobb was known for his surly demeanor and aggressive playing style, and had a propensity for sliding into bases with spikes high. Among his many individual accomplishments, he won 12 batting titles, was the American League most valuable player in 1911, stole home 54 times in his career, and hit .400 or better three times. He served as a captain in the army in 1918. Ty Cobb was a first-ballot hall-of-famer in 1936, receiving 98.2% of the vote.

title: BB-Gandil, Charles
description: Charles "Chick" Gandil (1888–1970) played first base for three American League teams in his major league career: the Washington Senators, Cleveland Indians, and Chicago White Sox. He was part of the 1917 White Sox World Series championship team. He was also the ringleader of the 1919 Black Sox scandal, the conspiracy to fix the 1919 World Series. Gandil made the key contact with the gambling outfit that paid off the eight players allegedly involved in throwing the series and, ultimately, being banned from baseball for life by Commissioner Landis. Separate of the scandal, his on-field performance as a major leaguer included leading the American League four times in fielding percentage as a first baseman. He batted .277 lifetime.

title: BB-Risberg, Charles
description: Charles “Swede” Risberg  (1894–1975) was a Major League Baseball shortstop. He played for the Chicago White Sox in 1917-1920, and was  member of the World Series champion White Sox in 1917. He was one of the ringleaders of the 1919 World Series Black Sox scandal, convincing some of his teammates to conspire to fix the series. Known as an outstanding fielder, Risberg made eight errors in the series, and had only two hits in 25 at-bats. He received a lifetime ban from major league baseball for his role in the fix. He continued to play semi-pro baseball for the next decade.

title: BB-Wambsganss, William
description: Shown here as a member of the Cleveland Indians, William Wambsganss (1894–1985) was a major league second baseman who played 10 years with the Indians, and later with Boston Red Sox, and Philadelphia Athletics in a 13-year career (1914-1926). The Cleveland, Ohio native hit .259 in 1,492 games, batting in 519 runs. He had only 375 errors in 8,064 chances in his career, posting a fielding percentage of .954. His best hitting season was the .295 he posted in 1918. He hit .290 in 1923, his last season with the Indians. In game five of the World Series in 1920 at League Park, “Wamby” turned the only unassisted triple play in World Series history. He died in Lakewood, Ohio in 1985 and was buried at Cavalry Cemetery in Cleveland.

title: P-Chase, Harold
description: Harold (Hal) Chase (1883-1947) played first base in his five-team, 14-year major league career, which included a 1905-1913 stretch with the New York Highlanders/Yankees. “Prince Hal” was a strong fielding first baseman, and posted a .291 career average, batting in 941 runs and stealing 363 bases. In 1916, as a member of the Cincinnati Reds, he led the National League in hitting with a .339 batting average. His stellar on-field play was offset by numerous allegations in his career regarding gambling on baseball and throwing games.

title: Larry Doby
description: Shown batting as a member of the Cleveland Indians, Larry Doby (1923-2003) was the first African-American player in the American League, making his debut with the Indians in July 1947. Doby and teammate Satchel Paige were the first African-American players to win a World Series championship, helping the Indians prevail in 1948. Also in that year, his first as the team's full-time centerfielder, Doby batted .301. During his career (1947-1959), he made the all-star team seven consecutive years, and hit 20 or more home runs in eight straight years, including 32 each in 1952 and 1954, when he led the American League. Larry Doby was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1998.

title: P-Felsch, Oscar
description: Oscar "Happy" Felsch (1891–1964) played centerfield for the Chicago White Sox in 1915-1920. A lifetime .293 hitter, he was a member of the World Series champion White Sox in 1917, batting in 102 runs that year. He was one of the eight players involved in the 1919 World Series Black Sox scandal, in which the players allegedly received payments from gamblers to throw the series. During the series, Felsch hit poorly and misplayed fly balls in center field, as the White Sox lost the series five games to three.

title: P-Gleason, William
description: Pictured here as the Chicago White Sox manager, William J. "Kid" Gleason (1866–1933) played for seven teams in the majors in 1888-1912 as a second baseman and pitcher. He managed the White Sox in 1919-1923. During his playing career, Gleason compiled 138 wins and 131 losses, and had four 20-win seasons. He batted .261 lifetime, with 1,946 hits and 824 RBI, hitting .300+ in three seasons. As a player, Gleason was a member of National League pennant winners in 1894 and 1895 with the Philadelphia Quakers. Gleason managed the Chicago White Sox in 1919-1923, and was the team’s manager in the 1919 World Series when the Black Sox Scandal took place. He was not involved in the alleged fix. After leaving the White Sox, Gleason was on the coaching staff for the Philadelphia Athletics until 1931.

title: P-Jackson, Joe (Shoeless)
description: Pictured here as a member of the Chicago White Sox, Shoeless Joe Jackson (1887-1951) was an outfielder with the Philadelphia Athletics, Cleveland Naps/Indians and White Sox in his 1908-1920 major league career. He was one of the all-time great hitters, batting .356 lifetime, with 1,772 hits and 785 runs batted in. As a rookie, he hit .408 with the A’s. Jackson was a member of the 1917 World Series champion White Sox. He is also known for his association with the Black Sox Scandal, in which some members of the 1919 White Sox conspired to fix the World Series, which the White Sox lost five games to three. Jackson was banned from Major League Baseball after the 1920 season by commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis. Jackson’s alleged guilt in the fix has been the subject of dispute over the years. In 1999, the The Sporting News' list of the 100 Greatest Baseball Players had him rated as number 35.

title: S-Cleveland-Sports-Baseball-Teams-Cleveland-Indians-1

Frank Duffy, the team's other shortstop, is to the right of Crosby. The unidentifiable player at the far right is probably starting pitcher Gaylord Perry.

title: S-Cleveland-Sports-Baseball-Teams-Cleveland-Indians-2
author: Dorksen, Robert E.
description: Cleveland Indians' righthander Dick Bosman (1994-) is mobbed by teammates and fans after throwing a no-hitter against the Oakland Athletics on July 19, 1974. Bosman played for four American League teams in his career, including the Indians in 1973-75. His career win-loss record was 82-85, with a 3.67 earned run average. As a member of the Washington Senators, he posted a league-leading ERA of 2.19 in 1969.

description: Left to right, Cleveland Indians starting pitchers in 1965: Luis Tiant, who posted a win-loss record of 11-11, Ralph Terry (11-6), Jack Kralick (5-11), & Sam McDowell (17-11), according to baseball-reference.com. The team's other starter, Sonny Siebert, had a win-loss record of 16-8. As a team, the Indians won 87 games and lost 75.

description: The photograph depicts the Cleveland Indians during the 1948 season. Pictured from left to right are: Thurman Tucker, Larry Doby, Lou Boudreau, Joe Gordon, Allie Clark, Eddie Robinson, Ken Keltner, Jim Hegan, and ace pitcher Bob Feller.The photograph is a copy made in 1974 for the Plain Dealer by Charles Harris.

title: S-Cleve-Bldgs-Dunn Field 01
description: In 1916, the Cleveland Indians' new team owner, 'Sunny Jim' Dunn, renamed the ballpark from League Park to Dunn Field. When Dunn died in 1922, his widow inherited the ballpark and the team. She sold the franchise in 1927, and the field became League Park again, according to Wikipedia.

title: Leroy (Satchel) Paige, 1971
description: The photograph depicts Leroy (Satchel) Paige at his induction into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Paige played for the Cleveland Indians in 1948 and 1949.

title: P-Mails, Walter-2
description: Shown here in his throwing motion as a member of the Cleveland Indians, left-handed pitcher John Walter 'Duster' Mails (1894–1974) pitched for three teams in his major league career: the Brooklyn Robins (1915–16), the Indians (1920–22), and St. Louis Cardinals (1925–26). He was on pennant winners in 1916, 1920 and 1926. In the 1920 World Series, he pitched a 1-0 complete game shutout of Brooklyn in Game 6. He also pitched 6.2 innings of relief in Game 3, giving up no runs. Mails' career record was 32 wins and 25 losses, with an ERA of 4.10, according to Wikipedia.

title: P-Marquard, Richard-1
description: Richard William "Rube" Marquard (1886–1980) was a left-handed pitcher in a Major League Baseball career that spanned the years 1908-25.  He pitched with the New York Giants (1908-15), Brooklyn Robins (1915-20), Cincinnati Reds (1921), and Boston Braves (1922-25). His career win-loss record was 201-177, with a 3.08 E.R.A. Marquard was a member of 5 National League pennant winners, in 1911, 1912, 1913, 1915 and 1920.  He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1971.

title: P-Mails, Walter-1
description: Left-handed pitcher John Walter 'Duster' Mails (1894–1974) pitched for three teams in his major league career: the Brooklyn Robins (1915–16), Cleveland Indians (1920–22), and St. Louis Cardinals (1925–26). He was on pennant winners in 1916, 1920 and 1926. In the 1920 World Series, he pitched a 1-0 complete game shutout of Brooklyn in Game 6. He also pitched 6.2 innings of relief in Game 3, giving up no runs. Mails' career record was 32 wins and 25 losses, with an ERA of 4.10, according to Wikipedia.

title: P-Sewell, Joe-1
description: Shown here in a New York Yankees uniform, Joe Sewell (1898–1990) was a shortstop with the Cleveland Indians (1920-30) and Yankees (1931-33). He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1977. Sewell struck out only 114 times in 7,132 career at-bats for an average of one strikeout every 62.5 at-bats, according to Wikipedia. In 1932, he struck out only three times. Over his career, he batted .312 with 1,141 runs and 1,055 RBI. He hit 49 home runs and had a .391 on-base percentage. He was a World Series champion on 1920 and 1932.

title: P-Speaker, Tris-2
author: Conlon, Charles M.
description: Shown here as a member of the Cleveland Indians, throwing from the outfield, Tristram E. (Tris) Speaker (1888–1958) excelled as both an offensive and defensive player in his long Major League Baseball career. The center fielder holds the major league record for assists, with 449. He hit .345 over his career, ranking sixth all-time. His 3,515 hits are fifth best, and his 792 doubles are tops in that category. Speaker played for the Boston Americans/Red Sox (1907-15), the Indians (1916-26, Washington Senators (1927), and Philadelphia Athletics (1928). He was a World Series champion three times: in 1912, 1915 and 1920. In 1912, he was the American League MVP, batting .383. Speaker was also a manager, holding that position with the Indians in 1919-26. He was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1937, according to Wikipedia.

title: P-Sewell, Joe-2
description: Shown here in a Cleveland Indians uniform, Joe Sewell (1898–1990) was a shortstop with the Indians (1920-30) and New York Yankees (1931-33). He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1977. Sewell struck out only 114 times in 7,132 career at-bats for an average of one strikeout every 62.5 at-bats, according to Wikipedia. In 1932, he struck out only three times.  Over his career, he batted .312 with 1,141 runs and 1,055 RBI. He hit 49 home runs and had a .391 on-base percentage. He was a World Series champion on 1920 and 1932.

title: S-Cleveland-Chapman, Raymond Johnson (Grave)
author: Greene, Marvin M.
description: The Lake View Cemetery grave site of Cleveland Indians shortstop Ray Chapman is pictured. According to the Plain Dealer, "Chapman was the Indians' brilliant shortstop who was hit in the left temple by a pitched ball thrown by Carl Mays in an Indians-Yankees game at the Polo Grounds on Aug. 16, 1920." Surgery was performed on Chapman later that night and he died the next morning. His death led Major League Baseball to establish a rule requiring umpires to replace the ball whenever it became dirty. It was thought that Chapman never saw the earthen-colored ball that hit him. His death was also partially the reason why the spitball was banned after the 1920 season. Batting helmets were not required in Major League Baseball until more than 30 years later. Chapman played his whole career (1912-20) with the Indians.
